archetype.name: Playoff Team (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A Jacksonville team whose defense smothers runs and short throws, with an efficient, low-turnover passing game. Its play is good enough for contender talk, though the schedule so far has been soft.

report.headline: Last year's luck has turned into real efficiency, led by a suffocating defense.
report.take:
The 2025 Jaguars went 13-4 on the league's biggest luck cushion: 3.87 wins over expectation, first in football, and a 70.6% cover rate. The natural worry for Liam Coen's second year was a fall back to earth. Instead the 2026 team is playing better than that one. Net EPA is up from 0.117 to 0.178 (3rd), the point differential is +10.6 a game (2nd), and the record sits only one win above what the scoring margin predicts. This 4-1 is mostly earned.

The engine is a defense that takes away the easy stuff. Opponents run for -0.227 EPA a carry (3rd) and throw short for -0.334 a play, the best mark in the league. Offenses have mostly stopped trying on the ground: they pass 5.8 points more often than normal against Jacksonville, and Cincinnati and Philadelphia ran for 23 and 22 yards. On offense, Trevor Lawrence is efficient rather than prolific (0.209 pass EPA, 7th) and spreads the ball: Parker Washington leads with 35 targets, Brenton Strange has 26, and Brian Thomas Jr. is only fourth with 17. Behind a line that gives the backs 1.9 yards before contact (28th), Bhayshul Tuten's 82 carries still produce the 8th-best rushing EPA.

The 14 points allowed a game overstate the defense a little. The yardage allowed is ordinary (330.6 a game, 16th). What keeps points off the board is a 33% red-zone touchdown rate (2nd) and eight takeaways, and both tend to drift back toward average. The vulnerability is deep: 0.839 EPA on deep throws (23rd), and Cincinnati put up 428 passing yards. Three of the five offenses faced rank 24th or worse by EPA. The last two wins came by a combined seven points, with 225 penalty yards. Those games also cost them starting tackle Anton Harrison and safety Eric Murray.

The path ahead is friendly. Four of the remaining 12 games are against Tennessee and Indianapolis, and the only opponent with a top-10 offense and a winning record is Baltimore. The division lead is already two games. Expect the defense to give up a few more points as the red-zone luck fades, but the efficiency base is strong enough to carry them to 11-13 wins and the AFC South.

strengths.title: Run and underneath defense is elite
strengths.body: Jacksonville allows the third-lowest rushing EPA and the league's lowest EPA on short passes. Opponents respond by abandoning the run. Being this good against both, plus a top-two explosive-run rate, points to sound fits and tackling rather than one-game flukes. It should hold, though it pushes offenses into the deep shots where this defense is weaker.

strengths.title: Efficient, clean passing offense
strengths.body: Lawrence's pass EPA ranks 7th, and the line allows pressure on just 15.8% of dropbacks (8th). He has three turnover-free or one-turnover games in a row, and the whole team is a level above last year's net EPA. Because the targets are spread out, no single coverage can take the offense away.

strengths.title: Run game beats its blocking
strengths.body: The backs get little room before contact (28th), yet rushing EPA ranks 8th. That gap means Tuten is creating yards himself, and it keeps the offense on schedule and the clock moving. Production that depends on the back is less stable than production that comes from blocking, so it may dip, especially if Harrison misses time.

concerns.title: Points allowed flattered by red zone
concerns.body: A 33% red-zone touchdown rate and eight takeaways are doing a lot of work for a defense that allows league-average yardage. Both numbers tend to regress toward the middle. Expect points allowed to climb from 14 toward the high teens even if the per-play efficiency holds.

concerns.title: Deep ball is the soft spot
concerns.body: The flip side of shutting down everything short is a 23rd-ranked EPA on deep throws, and Cincinnati exposed it for 428 yards. Secondary depth is now thin: Eric Murray is out with a concussion and Montaric Brown is questionable. This is a real structural weakness, not noise, and patient quarterbacks will keep testing it.

concerns.title: Penalties and hits on Lawrence
concerns.body: The last two games cost 125 and 100 penalty yards. The line lets Lawrence get hit at the 28th-ranked rate despite good pressure numbers, which partly reflects how long he holds the ball (25th in time to throw). Losing Harrison, a 92%-snap starter, makes both problems worse.

trend.note: Margins of +24, -7, +29, +5 and +2 show the blowouts giving way to tighter, sloppier wins. Even so, the passing EPA has risen each of the last three weeks, and the defense held its last two opponents to 45 rushing yards combined.

nextGame.headline: Houston's broken run game walks into Jacksonville's best strength
nextGame.body:
Houston is better than 1-4. Its net EPA ranks 14th, it sits 1.91 wins under expectation, and it is 0-for-close-games. But its profile is close to the worst possible fit for this opponent. The Texans average 3.03 yards a carry (32nd) into the league's third-best run defense, which leaves C.J. Stroud to beat a defense that wins underneath. Stroud's route to points is time in the pocket and deep shots at a secondary missing Murray. On the other side, Houston's pass defense is leaky outside, with 26th in deep EPA and opposing WR1s scoring 6.5 PPR points over their average. That suits Washington and an offense that already passes efficiently.

Availability tilts toward Jacksonville. Houston's lead back David Montgomery and starting safety Jalen Pitre (92% of snaps) are both doubtful, and tackle Braden Smith is on IR. Jacksonville's big question is Harrison, whose absence would matter against a rush with 18 sacks. The Jaguars are also coming off a London game on normal rest, and the long snapper is questionable. The early forecast shows 14 mph wind with gusts near 28. It is five days out, but if it holds it would cut into the deep game on both sides.

keyMatchups.title: Texans pass rush vs Harrison-less line
keyMatchups.body: Houston has the second-most sacks in football and a 9% sack rate, while Jacksonville already allows the 28th-ranked hit rate. If Harrison can't go and Lawrence holds the ball, this is how Houston steals the game. Quick game and play-action will be the counter.

keyMatchups.title: Houston's ground game vs a brick wall
keyMatchups.body: The league's worst rushing offense by yards per carry meets a defense allowing -0.227 EPA per run, and Houston's lead back is doubtful. That should make Houston one-dimensional early.

keyMatchups.title: Washington against a leaky back end
keyMatchups.body: Houston has given lead receivers 6.5 PPR points over their average and ranks 26th on deep throws, and Pitre is likely out. Washington's target lead makes him the natural beneficiary, wind permitting.

nextGame.watch: Whether Harrison plays, and whether Jacksonville protects Lawrence against Houston's 9% sack rate without him.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is real and the schedule is soft. Two games each against Tennessee (31st offense) and Indianapolis, plus Houston twice, should keep the Jaguars comfortably ahead in the AFC South. The road trips to Baltimore and Dallas are the clearest risks, and Dallas's 4th-ranked offense is exactly the kind that can attack this secondary deep. Expect the passing game to stay around its current level, with steady volume from Lawrence.

The parts to discount are the 33% red-zone defense and the +1 turnover margin a game. As those normalize, points allowed should rise into the high teens and a couple of close games will go the other way. The bigger variables are health: Harrison on the line, and the safety and cornerback depth behind a defense whose weakness is already deep coverage.
swingFactors: Anton Harrison's knee and pass protection
Secondary health against deep passing teams

bets.reason: Jacksonville's net EPA (0.178) dwarfs Houston's (0.019), and the point-differential gap is about 11 a game. Houston's 32nd-ranked rushing attack runs straight into Jacksonville's strength without its lead back. The risk keeping this from higher is Houston's pass rush facing a line that may be missing Harrison.

Jacksonville games have averaged 38.6 combined points, and four of five went under. Houston can't run and faces a defense that kills short passes, while its own defense ranks 4th in success rate. The early gusty forecast is a small extra push toward the under.

confidence.note: Five games, three against bottom-third offenses, but the efficiency is consistent and up on last year.
